fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Memucan asks that the decree be recorded in the laws of Persia and Media “…so that it cannot be repealed…” (Esther 1:19). That means the statement is true as written. Once it's in, it stays in. No take-backs.

The military leaders of Persia and Media were at the earlier feast (Esther 1:3). This garden court feast is a different one. The king invites all the people in the citadel of Susa, “…from the least to the greatest.” (Esther 1:5) That isn't limited to the military leaders.

Not quite, friend. The text says the drinks were served in an array of goblets of gold, each with a different design (Esther 1:7). That's gold goblets, but every one has its own look. No matching set here.

A one goblet rule would put a limit on the drinking, and the text says the opposite. The king ordered that no limit was placed on the drinking (Esther 1:8). The royal wine flowed freely. One each is more of a cookie-tasting rule than a royal one.

The text says every official of his household was to serve each man whatever he desired (Esther 1:8). So it isn't only what the king pours. The order was that no limit was placed on the drinking. I'd say the king had plenty of help.
Right, friend. Queen Vashti gives a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Xerxes (Esther 1:9). The king has his feast, and the queen has a banquet of her own. Her guest list is the women.

The servants were at the king's first feast, along with his officials (Esther 1:3). Vashti's banquet is for a different group. The text says it's for the women in the royal palace (Esther 1:9). Different guest list.
The princes of the provinces were guests at the king's feast (Esther 1:3). Queen Vashti's banquet is for the women in the royal palace (Esther 1:9). The queen hosted a banquet of her own.

Yes, friend. The king orders the eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing her royal crown (Esther 1:11). That's a summons with a dress code attached. Crown required, and he put it right in the order.

That's it. Queen Vashti refuses to come at the king's command brought by his eunuchs (Esther 1:12). The text doesn't give her reason, so I won't make one up. The command came by the eunuchs, and her answer was no.

Serving at a feast isn't in his plan. Memucan says the decree should state “…that Vashti shall never again enter the presence of King Xerxes…” (Esther 1:19). That's about the king's presence, and serving at a feast isn't mentioned. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

That's it, friend. Memucan says the edict will be heard throughout the vast kingdom, “…and so all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands.” (Esther 1:20) That's what he says will follow from the edict. The text doesn't tell us how it turns out.

Leaving isn't in what Memucan says here, friend. He says the edict will be heard throughout the vast kingdom, “…and so all women, from the least to the greatest, will honor their husbands.” (Esther 1:20) Honoring their husbands is what he says all women will do. Nothing about leaving households.

That's right. The king and his princes were pleased with this counsel, so the king did as Memucan advised (Esther 1:21). The king acted on the advice he was given. Memucan's counsel became the king's move.

That's not what the text says. He sent letters to all the provinces, “…to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language…” (Esther 1:22). With 127 provinces, I bet that was a lot of copying. Writing the same letter once is enough work for me.

You got it. The king sent letters to all the provinces, “…to each province in its own script and to each people in their own language…” (Esther 1:22). So the letters went out in the languages of the different peoples. That's a whole lot of writing from one royal pen.
